10566-the-bequest-ship-s-company-part-6:
W. W. Jacobs built Ship's Company from short comic stories about sailors and small-town life, and "The Bequest" is one of its tales. Robert Clarkson has waited some thirty years for the woman he once courted, while his lifelong rival stood in his way. When the rival dies, a visitor arrives with news that changes what Clarkson may now expect.

Jacobs tells the story through quiet talk by the fire, with dry humor in every exchange. Clarkson weighs patience, loyalty, and hope against the awkward facts of a dead man's wishes. The tale gives readers a gentle, funny look at long waiting, old rivalry, and the surprises that can follow a will.
10786-odd-man-out-sailor-s-knots-part-6:
W. W. Jacobs's "Odd Man Out," the sixth tale in Sailors' Knots from 1909, opens with the night-watchman denouncing friendship as a delusion and a snare. He has had more friendships than most, he says, and nearly all ended suddenly. One friend who once thought he could do no wrong now makes a face at him in the street.

The break came when the friend, uneasy about marrying, asked how his looks would strike the watchman if he were a girl. Honest praise of heart, temper, and purse did not save the friendship. Readers get a funny monologue on truth, vanity, and the odd ways friendships end.
11186-over-the-side-captains-all-book-6:
W. W. Jacobs wrote this short sea tale, Over the Side, sixth in the Captains All series. The narrator argues that seamen are prone to superstition, afloat on black waste waters with vast depths below, where belief in the supernatural comes easier than ashore under cheerful gas-lamps. An incident from his own experience made him chary of calling a man fool or coward for encountering something he cannot explain.

At fifteen, his father refusing to apprentice him to the sea, he shipped before the mast on the brig Endeavour, bound for Riga, and attached himself to Bill Smith. Jem Dadd, a morose man of forty, claimed rats were the souls of drowned sailors and frightened his fellows with supernatural tales. One night a dark figure springs over the side onto the deck, and Bill roars as never before. Jacobs mixes ghost story with shipboard humour.
11364-clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of:
Volume six of Samuel Richardson's Clarissa Harlowe, in a nine-volume edition, continues the heroine's story entirely in letters, from letter one through letter seventy-three. Detailed contents show Lovelace writing to Belford about conditional promises to Tomlinson, pleas on their situation, a whimsical contest with his conscience. A meeting with Clarissa in the garden, where her composure and noble conversation refuse him any determination in his favor.

Richardson's epistolary method lets readers follow Clarissa's moral struggle from inside, letter by letter, with Lovelace's self-deception exposed in his own words. This middle volume deepens the novel's central conflict without resolving it. Readers tackling Clarissa will find volume six essential to its tragic arc.
11452-stories-by-american-authors-volume:
Stories by American Authors, volume six from 1891, collects six stories: C. H. White's Village Convict, A. A. Hayes's Denver Express, Lina Redwood Fairfax's Misfortunes of Bro' Thomas Wheatley, L. W. Champney's Heartbreak Cameo, Albert Webster's Miss Eunice's Glove, and Harold Frederic's Brother Sebastian's Friendship. White's opener finds fishermen around a country-store stove discussing Eph, just out of state's prison after burning Eliphalet's barn, having first led the animals out.

Sympathy for Eph, a high-strung boy whose mother Eliphalet foreclosed on in winter, complicates the village's fear. The volume's stories share a regional, character-driven manner. Readers of American local color will find the collection a solid sample of magazine fiction before realism hardened.
11476-husbandry-deep-waters-part-6:
Jacobs's Deep Waters story Husbandry opens with the watchman's comparison: dealing with a man is easy as a teetotaller on a wide pavement. dealing with a woman like the same teetotaller after whiskies trying to climb a step that is not there. A young husband reports his wife's row in stages: cooing and moustache-pulling, temper and remarks about his sister. a banged door felling a vase, four returns with fresh grievances, refusal of food, and a secret supper of loaf, butter, and chops.

The husband's relief at her appetite earns a charge of grudging her food. Jacobs's humor is dated in its gender comedy, but its structure, escalation by anecdote, remains effective. The story is a compact example of his marital farce, told entirely in the watchman's voice.
11956-a-popular-history-of-france-from-t:
Volume 6 of Guizot's History of France, the last of the series, runs from Louis XIV and his court through his death in 1711 to 1715. It then turns to Louis XV, the Regency, and Cardinal Dubois from 1715 to 1723. Later chapters cover the ministry of Cardinal Fleury, France in the colonies from 1745 to 1763, and the Seven Years' War under the Duke of Choiseul.

Guizot closes his long narrative with the monarchy at its height and in decline, as court splendor, ministerial government, colonial rivalry, and European war strained the old regime. The volume's sweep, from Versailles to Canada and India, shows a historian thinking about France as a world power, not merely as a kingdom.
12126-in-the-library-the-lady-of-the-bar:
Two bachelors share a house and a firm in In the Library, a dark short story from W. W. Jacobs Lady of the Barge. Trayton Burleigh and James Fletcher inherited the place from a distant connection, and the partnership has curdled into hatred.

Fletcher, smoking his pipe in the third-floor library, tells Burleigh he must leave house and firm by morning, or face ruin. Burleigh weighs refusal, revenge, and flight through a long, wet night, listening to steps on the stairs and fearing what waits in the dark. Jacobs, usually comic, writes here a tense study of blackmail and pride. The library fire burns low as the two men play out a quiet war of nerves.
12156-the-three-sisters-night-watches-pa:
On a wet autumn evening thirty years before the tale begins, Ursula Mallow dies at Mallett Lodge and makes her sisters promise to lock her room and never open it. That vow drives The Three Sisters, the ghost story in W. W. Jacobs Night Watches.

Tabitha, hard and skeptical, keeps the room shut, while Eunice, the youngest, fears Ursula will return as she promised, to watch over them both. Strange sounds, a locked door, and a cat that cannot explain them wear Eunice down to fainting. Jacobs, master of the comic twist, here writes true unease: the ghost may be real, or may be guilt and grief in an old house. The ending leaves the reader, like Tabitha, unsure what to believe.
12206-breaking-a-spell-odd-craft-part-6:
Claybury folk never took much count of witchcraft, says the old narrator of Breaking a Spell, a comic tale from W. W. Jacobs Odd Craft. The exception is Joe Barlcomb, a newcomer who believes half the old ladies in town are witches and treats them with nervous politeness.

When Barlcomb wife breaks her leg and his luck sours, he seeks a wise woman, Mrs. Prince, for a cure. Her remedy is a midnight riddle: sell six men a ha penny for a shilling, and the man who makes the most fuss is the one who hexed him. Barlcomb midnight rounds turn suspicion into farce. Jacobs uses village superstition to mock fear itself, showing how a man can hex himself with worry.
21864-journeys-through-bookland-vol-6:
Great poems and tales for young readers fill this sixth volume of Journeys Through Bookland, Charles H. Sylvester's guided tour of the world's best literature for children, in its 1922 edition. Macaulay's Horatius opens the volume, the Roman legend of the bridge retold in ringing verse. Campbell's Lord Ullin's Daughter and The Rainbow follow, then a life of Sir Walter Scott and Scott's own Tournament.

Livingstone meets a lion, Byron destroys Sennacherib, and Tennyson sings Sweet and Low further in. A Kempis, John Brown's Rab and His Friends, and Annie Laurie round out the mix. Sylvester frames each piece for a child reader, with notes and care. The set aimed to walk children into real literature by a pleasant road, volume by volume.
21938-the-works-of-john-knox-volume-1-of:
Scotland's Reformation is told by its fiercest maker in this first volume of the Works of John Knox. David Laing edited it for the Wodrow Society. The editors chose to begin with Knox's History of the Reformation in Scotland, his work of greatest weight. Theodore Beza's Latin greeting heads the volume, calling Knox a kind of apostle of true worship in Scotland. Book one runs from 1494 to 1558, book two through 1559.

Appendices study the Lollards, Patrick Hamilton, and early martyrs under James the Fifth. Knox writes as a participant with a trumpet voice: sermons, plots, and burnings pass in review. The 1895 Edinburgh edition gathers his text with care. As history it is partisan; as a voice of the age, it has no equal in Scotland.
3852-memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-mo:
Madame de Montespan's sixth book marks the cooling of the king's favor. Louis, consoled for the death of the Duchesse de Fontanges, no longer returns to the sweet intimacy of eleven or twelve years. He approaches Montespan as one visits an acquaintance, with their children as the only bond. He then sets off on a splendid progress in Picardy and Flanders, and Montespan is not invited to join the boudoir navy.

The king relates the journey's delights to her afterward, while his Chambers of Reunion at Metz and Brisach strip great proprietors of lands once held from Alsace. A later passage shows Madame de Maintenon deftly steering the king on court fashions and a delayed demolition. The volume reads as a farewell to power, told by the woman losing it.
3952-cinq-mars-volume-6:
Alfred de Vigny's sixth volume of Cinq Mars turns to a monk questioned about love. The questioner demands what love is, confessing he knows nothing about it himself. The monk stands astounded, looks on the ground with the stupid eye of some base animal, and after long consideration answers in a drawling nasal voice.

Love must be a kind of malignant fever leading the brain astray, he says, though in truth he has never reflected on it until this moment. He has always been embarrassed speaking to a woman, and wishes women could be omitted from society altogether. Their one use, he says, is to disclose secrets, like the little Duchess or Marion de Lorme, whom he recommends to his Eminence. Readers who like Vigny's irony will find a volume of conspiracy told through comic ignorance.
4106-the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1:
Azel Ames's Mayflower history reaches its sixth volume with the journal of the ship herself, under Master Thomas Jones, from London toward Hudson's River in Virginia. The voyage began at London, as her consort's had at Delfshaven, and the journal tracks wind, weather, and landfall.

Ames sets the log beside the story of the company, noting where the larger ship's fortunes touched the smaller's. The volume gives readers the voyage day by day, in the master's own course. It suits those who want the crossing itself, not only the story around it.
4411-the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-volum:
Book Six of George Meredith's Ordeal of Richard Feverel opens on a southwestern island in a season of wind and rain, where Lord Mountfalcon still lingers to his friends' disgust. Mount's in for it again, they say among themselves, and the phrase hangs over the book's closing acts. Clare's diary and Austin's return follow.

The chapters promise nature speaking, the magian conflict again, and the last scene, with a letter from Lady Blandish to Austin Wentworth. Richard's ordeal reaches its tragic end here, as his father's system, his marriage, and his loves collide. This final volume completes Meredith's most famous novel of education and its failure.
4418-sandra-belloni-volume-6:
Book Six of George Meredith's Sandra Belloni opens with Emilia stretching out her hand to say goodbye. A hardened girl with dead eyelids does not seem to feel herself at the speaker's mercy, and the farewell carries the weight of the novel's long courtship. Despair, the book's first chapter title, sets the tone.

Later chapters bring Emilia found, the defection of Mr. Pericles from the Brookfield circle, Wilfrid kindling, and the hippogriff in air and on earth. The rape of the black-briony wreath, a call to action, and a further view of sentiment follow. This volume moves Emilia from despair toward a decision, with Meredith's irony intact.
4432-evan-harrington-volume-6:
Book Six of George Meredith's Evan Harrington opens on a summer evening, with dowagers firmly planted on Olympus. Warm colors lie along the grass, reddening pine stems and yellowing aspen leaves. A picnic hangs in doubt after two rude shocks, but happily survives, and the comedy of rank resumes.

The book's chapters promise Evan's light beginning to twinkle again, the hero taking his rank in the orchestra, a pagan sacrifice, and Rose wounded. Before breakfast and the retreat from Beckley follow, with a chapter on seeing in the dark. Evan's fortunes turn here, as love and birth pull him in opposite directions.
4440-vittoria-volume-6:
Book Six of George Meredith's Vittoria turns to episodes of the revolt and the war, opening with the tobacco riots and Rinaldo Guidascarpi. Anna von Lenkenstein, Meredith notes, could wait for vengeance, while Lena acts at once and harms herself most of all. Lena has broken her engagement with Wilfrid, and the cost is plain.

Later chapters tell the five days of Milan, Vittoria disobeying her lover, and the treachery of Pericles, with the white umbrella and the death of Rinaldo Guidascarpi. The book gives the revolution in episodes, mixing street fighting with private betrayals. Vittoria's voice and her choices carry the history.
4449-the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-vo:
Book Six of George Meredith's Adventures of Harry Richmond opens with Harry seeing his father taking the tide, and being carried on it himself. His father's meeting with his grandfather follows, with the commencement of the splendors and perplexities of the grand parade. The Marquis of Edbury and his puppet appear.

Harry becomes one of the chosen of the nation, and his father is miraculously relieved by fortune. The adventurer's schemes reach their height here, with Harry swept along in triumph and doubt. Meredith's comedy of a charming rogue and his loving son turns serious, as fortune's gifts prove double-edged.
4458-beauchamp-s-career-volume-6:
Book Six of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career turns on two passions in Nevil Beauchamp, and on the Earl of Romfrey and the countess. The earl's nephews show another exhibition of those passions in Beauchamp himself, and a little plot against Cecilia follows. As it might have been foreseen, the plot ends in refusal.

Beauchamp, naval officer turned radical, has fought for principle through elections, newspapers, and love affairs. This volume tests his constancy once more, as family pressure and Cecilia's fate press upon him. Meredith's political novel narrows toward its close, with honor and affection still at odds.
5239-the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-:
Charles James Lever's Harry Lorrequer concludes in this sixth volume, covering chapters forty-two through fifty-five. Journeys, a reminiscence of the East, a day in the Phoenix, an adventure in Canada, a courier's passport, a night in Strasbourg, a surprise. Jack Waller's story carries Harry toward the end of his confessions.

The volume holds only this final stretch, and its far-flung episodes show Lever's hero still travelling, still confessing, and still finding trouble. Readers finishing the novel here get its closing adventures, from Canada to the Continent, in the comic voice that carried the whole book.
5813-following-the-equator-a-journey-aro:
Part six of Mark Twain's Following the Equator covers chapters fifty-one through sixty, in India. Chapter fifty-one opens with a Pudd'nhead Wilson maxim about making a nation's superstitions, then declares Benares a big church, a religious hive whose every cell is a temple, shrine, or mosque. Every earthly and heavenly good, Twain jokes, is procurable under one roof.

Twain offers his India at its most vivid: temples, pilgrims, priests, and street life rendered with humor and sharp observation. The part balances wonder at devotion with skepticism about superstition and exploitation. It suits readers who enjoy Twain's Indian chapters, and it offers a memorable, opinionated portrait of Benares and the religious life of a great city.
5823-the-gilded-age-part-6:
Part six of The Gilded Age, by Twain and Warner, covers chapters forty-six through fifty-four, opening on a bright spring morning in Washington. Philip leaves the Capitol walking up Pennsylvania Avenue with Senator Dilworthy, amid soft air, deepening green, pink peach blossom, and the warm south wind. The annual renewal of the city frames a season of lobbying, love, and political maneuver.

Readers see the novel's Washington at its most vivid, as Philip navigates senators, schemes, and personal hopes. The part balances romance with satire, letting spring beauty contrast with the grubby business of influence. It suits readers nearing the novel's climax, since alliances formed on this walk will shape trials and fortunes ahead.
5841-sketches-new-and-old-part-6:
Part six of Mark Twain's Sketches New and Old opens with The Undertaker's Chat, in which an undertaker pats the folded hands of the deceased approvingly. The corpse, he says, was a brick every way you took him, real accommodating, modest-like and simple in his last moments. Friends wanted a metallic burial case, but the dead man's modesty shapes the joke that follows.

Here Twain gives his dark humor at its most characteristic, finding comedy in funerals without cruelty to the dead. The part gathers further sketches where death, business, and human vanity meet in deadpan talk. It suits readers who enjoy Twain's gallows humor, and it shows how a single voice, the undertaker's, can carry a whole sketch.
5859-personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-vo:
Volume two, part six of Sheridan's Personal Memoirs covers chapters twelve through twenty, on the postwar frontier. Headings treat Fort Leavenworth, the Treaty of Medicine Lodge, going to Fort Dodge, discontented Indians, Indian outrages, a delegation of chiefs, and a terrible raid. The death of Comstock, vast herds of buffalo, a winter campaign, and meeting Buffalo Bill follow.

Readers get Sheridan's account of plains service after the Civil War, with Forsyth's gallant fight and rescue closing the section. The memoir favors operational detail and frontier incident, told in a general's plain prose. Modern readers should note its period language about Native peoples, while historians will value its firsthand view of treaties, raids, and campaigns.
5865-personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-:
Part six of Grant's Personal Memoirs covers chapters sixty-two through seventy, in the war's final months. Headings treat Sherman's march north, Sheridan ordered to Lynchburg, Canby ordered against Mobile, and movements of Schofield and Thomas. The capture of Columbia, South Carolina, and Sherman in the Carolinas follow, while news of Sherman in possession of Savannah draws statesmen and visitors north.

Grant gives his closing account of coordinated campaigns, as armies converge and the Confederacy's end approaches. The memoir records orders, movements, and meetings with the same plain clarity as earlier volumes. It suits Civil War readers finishing Grant's story, and it offers a commander's view of victory without triumphalism, focused on duty done.
6235-the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-:
The bell of the Cohue Royale clatters on the fourth of October for the opening of the Assise d'Heritage. The court fills with governor, bailly, jurats, seigneurs, and avocats learned in Norman custom. The Royal Court and the States will welcome Admiral Prince Philip d'Avranche, Duc de Bercy, and offer a bounty to Jerseymen enlisting under him. The island is en fete, alive with a year of sensations unmatched since the Battle of Jersey.

This final volume brings the long story to its courtroom close, where law, honour, and island custom meet in public. Parker also gives a harrowing climb, fingers gripping rock on a limestone shelf, as a body draws itself up from a granite wall. Ceremony and peril share the stage, and the romance ends with Jersey itself, its courts, its people, and its sea, in full view.
7138-the-great-conspiracy-volume-6:
Logan's sixth part of The Great Conspiracy opens at chapter twenty two, Freedom's Sun Still Rising, after Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation. Friends of freedom saw clearly, none more than Lincoln himself, that until that great act entered the Constitution itself, no real assurance guarded the liberties of the emancipated. Without it, even after rebellion's suppression, a living spark of dissension might at any time fan again into civil war.

At all proper times Lincoln favored and urged congressional action, but definite action began only the following year, and Congress moved slow. In his third annual message Lincoln pledged he would not attempt to retract or modify the proclamation while he remained in his position. Only this sixth part's course is followed here, as emancipation seeks constitutional ground.
7159-the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-6:
Part six of Twain's Prince and the Pauper opens at chapter eighteen, The Prince with the Tramps, as the troop of vagabonds turns out at early dawn. A lowering sky hangs overhead, sloppy ground lies underfoot, and winter chill fills the air, with all gaiety gone from the company. Some stand sullen, some irritable, none gentle humored, all thirsty. The Ruffler puts Jack in Hugo's charge with brief instructions. He commands John Canty to keep away and let him alone, and warns Hugo not to be too rough with the lad.

After a while weather grows milder and clouds lift somewhat. The troop stops shivering as spirits improve. They grow more cheerful, then chaff each other and insult passengers, waking again to life's joys. The dread in which their sort is held shows in how everybody gives them room. Only this part's march is followed here.
7198-the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-6:
Part Six of Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer stirs the sleepy village with the murder trial, which becomes the absorbing topic of all talk at once. Tom cannot escape it, and every mention sends a shudder through him, since his troubled conscience half persuades him that remarks in his hearing are feelers meant to test him. He does not see how he could be suspected, yet comfort eludes him.

Tom takes Huck to a lonely place for a talk, seeking relief in unsealing his tongue for a little while. The trial scenes turn village gossip into a moral pressure chamber, with fear and loyalty pulling the boys in opposite ways. This part holds the trial's opening grip and Tom's private dread.
7247-a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur:
Part Six of Mark Twain's Connecticut Yankee sends the Yankee and the king travelling incognito, and the disguise begins with hair. High classes wear hair banged across the forehead and hanging to the shoulders, low commoners are banged fore and aft, and slaves go bangless with free growth. The Yankee inverts a bowl over the king's head and cuts away all that hangs below it.

Whiskers and moustache follow, trimmed to a villainous half-inch and done inartistically on purpose, so the king can pass as lowly. Twain turns a barber's job into a lesson in rank, showing how much of majesty hangs on a haircut. This part holds the making of the disguise and the road that follows.
736-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
Edward Gibbon devoted this sixth volume, with notes by H. H. Milman, to the Crusades and their aftermath in the East. It opens with the Crusades themselves, then the Fourth Crusade, which turned its arms against fellow Christians and sacked Constantinople. The partition of the empire by French and Venetians follows.

Gibbon traces how the crusading age weakened the Byzantine state and reshaped trade and power in the Mediterranean. His judgement is cool and ironic, sparing neither popes nor princes. The volume is vital for readers who want the long view of the Crusades, not just battles, but the slow unravelling of an empire.
7755-godolphin-volume-6:
Constance reproaches herself in the final volume of Lytton's Godolphin, after betraying before another man how much she leans on her husband's heart. Her conscience alarms her at the slip, yet she cannot quell delight at Radclyffe's solemn word that Godolphin still loves her.

Radclyffe, austere and sincere, presses her to ask whether she too neglected him in return, and whether softness might have won what pride lost. She turns the question over without rest, weighing her own conduct against his. The closing volume brings a marriage to honest reckoning, where love survives only through plain self-knowledge.
8476-life-on-the-mississippi-part-6:
Part 6 of Life on the Mississippi opens with chapter 26, Under Fire, as talk turns to war. Twain's boat moves down into the upper edge of the former battle stretch, with Columbus just behind, and much is said about the famous battle of Belmont. Several officers aboard had seen active service in the Mississippi war fleet, and their talk fills the chapter.

This section shows the river as a war zone remembered, with veterans' stories correcting romantic notions. Readers get Twain's Civil War river, not as history but as boat talk, with officers who found themselves sadly out of step with glory. It is the book in its reminiscent, slightly skeptical vein.
8706-the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-6:
Gustave Dore's sixth Bible volume tells the early life and ministry of Jesus, passage by passage beside the engravings. It opens with the Nativity: Caesar Augustus decrees a taxing, Joseph travels from Nazareth to Bethlehem, and Mary lays her firstborn in a manger. The star in the East, the flight into Egypt, and the massacre of the innocents follow, then the boy Jesus questioning the doctors in the Temple.

Healing the sick, the Sermon on the Mount, stilling the tempest, and the disciples plucking corn on the Sabbath show the teacher and healer at work. Dore's pictures, even unseen, are suggested by the scale of the chosen scenes. The volume works as a short gospel harmony for family or devotional reading, and as a record of how the nineteenth century pictured the life of Christ.
895-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
This sixth and final volume of Gibbon's history carries the story to the fall of Constantinople and beyond. It treats the Crusades, the Fourth Crusade's sack of the Christian capital, and the partition of the empire by French and Venetians, then the long Turkish advance that ends the Byzantine state.

Gibbon closes his vast work with a survey of what survived Rome: laws, churches, and cities, and the new nations that rose on Roman ground. Milman's notes complete the edition. The volume is the fitting end to a great history, where the fall that began with Antonines reaches its last, eastern close.
9448-samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-:
A letter from Miss Timson sends Samantha to Loontown in this sixth part of Marietta Holley's Samantha Among the Brethren. Written on the sixth day of a sickness, it brings Josiah and Samantha sailing the next day after it arrives. The sisters of the meeting house counsel her to go, since Sister Bobbet's fall on apple paring halted the papering work.

The interests of Zion, they agree, will not languish for a day or two, and duty calls Samantha plainly. Divisions arise only over which road to take. Holley's dialect comedy carries a serious point about women's work. The part remains a delightful close to the Brethren sequence.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co:
Part 6 cuts King Arthur's hair with a bowl, dresses him in a peasant's coarse brown robe, and sends him travelling incognito with Hank to learn his kingdom at ground level. The king must be drilled to stoop, shuffle, and keep the pride out of his voice, and he fails at nearly every cottage door they try.

On the road they find a smallpox hut where a dying mother curses the lord who jailed her husband, and a manor-house tragedy of lords and priests that destroys a whole family. At Marco's cottage the disguised king hears how his taxes and laws look from below. Twain's comedy darkens here into an indictment of the order Arthur rules.
ante-nicene-fathers-vol-6:
Volume six of the Ante-Nicene Fathers gathers the third century's second rank: Gregory Thaumaturgus, Dionysius the Great, Julius Africanus, Anatolius, and the minor writers, with Methodius and Arnobius. Roberts and Donaldson edited the set in 1885. Several of these names survive in fragments only.

Gregory the wonder-worker was Origen's pupil, and his address of thanks to his teacher is a gem of ancient education. Dionysius of Alexandria writes letters through plague and persecution. Julius Africanus, the first Christian chronographer, tries to date the world. Arnobius, a pagan convert, closes the volume mocking the gods he once served. The volume is a museum of the church's growing mind.
arabian-nights-payne-1883-vol-6:
Volume VI of Payne's Thousand Nights and One Night, from 1883, brings more nights from the Calcutta Arabic text. The unexpurgated Englishing that made John Payne's version the first complete one continues here at full length. Shahrazad's voice, calm under threat of death, frames every marvel that follows.

Readers of the full set prize this sameness-in-variety: the same spell, new wonders each night. Demons, treasures, and sudden reversals of fortune crowd the pages as ever. Volume VI carries the design forward with three volumes left, Burton's famous rival still standing on its claim of completeness.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-6:
Volume six of Michael L. Rodkinson's English Babylonian Talmud pairs Tract Yoma with Tract Hagiga. Yoma is the tractate of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year. Hagiga treats the festival offerings brought by pilgrims to Jerusalem.

Yoma follows the high priest through his long day: his washings, his confessions, the scapegoat sent to the desert, and his entry into the Holy of Holies. Hagiga then weighs who must appear at the feasts and what offerings count. The volume holds the Temple's most solemn rite and its most joyful gatherings side by side. Rodkinson's notes guide readers through both.
bancroft-history-us-vol-6:
Valley Forge and the French alliance mark the sixth volume of Bancroft's History, from 1860. The Revolution's middle years bring hunger, doubt, and then a turning tide. Aid from France lifts the cause when it most needs hope.

Bancroft wrote as America slid toward its own civil war. He found in the old trials a mirror and a warning for his time. Endurance under want becomes his great theme here. The volume shows the Revolution surviving its darkest stretch, held together by Washington's will and the people's refusal to quit a cause they had made their own.
beauchamp-s-career-volume-6:
Volume six of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career covers chapters forty-two to forty-nine. Two passions, love and family pride, rule the opening. The Earl of Romfrey and his countess confront Nevil's entanglement with Renée, the French wife of his youth. Her boxes, her hotel, and her remembered sentences haunt him.

A little plot against Cecilia Halkett thickens the rivalry between the women. The Earl faces a trial of his own as baronial despotism, the old family tyranny, begins to crumble. Nevil's nephews and cousins expose the Romfrey temper at full stretch. Meredith drives his political novel toward private reckoning. Honour, obstinacy, and affection collide in these chapters, written in his most compressed and glittering style.
carlyle-friedrich-vol-6:
Sans Souci and quiet years close Carlyle's vast life of Frederick in this sixth volume, from 1897. The old king rules as an enlightened despot, builds, judges cases, and plays the flute. Death comes at last to the palace he loved best.

Six volumes end with the hero's calm exit from the stage. Carlyle's obsession with his subject never flags across decades of work. Law, farming, and philosophy fill the king's late days here. following-the-equator-a-journey-around-t:
Following the Equator, Part 6, by Mark Twain, walks the pilgrim road at Benares, the holy city on the Ganges. Twain calls the city, in effect, one big church, its every cell a temple, shrine, or mosque, stocked like a great store with every earthly and heavenly good. His chapter opens with a calendar maxim about superstition and law, then lays out an itinerary for the visitor.

Step one is purification: bathe in the Ganges at sunrise, pray, and drink some of the water. Step two guards against hunger at the Cow Temple, and the list proceeds through the city's sacred economy with guidebook precision, drawn from a local guide and a missionary's conversation. Twain is respectful of the devotion and merciless about the system built on it, a double vision that powers the Indian chapters of his voyage.
freeman-norman-conquest-vol-6:

Serious readers use this volume to check Freeman's bold claims. Students find in it a map of the chronicles and charters he mined. The labor is dry, yet it is the bedrock of the whole structure. Few Victorian histories show their working so fully, and the volume honors an age when a historian proved his case in public, note by note.
froude-history-england-vol-6:
Two queens duel across the sixth volume of Froude's History of England, issued in eighteen sixty. Elizabeth holds England while Mary Stuart, captive and plotting, claims its crown. Their long contest ends at last on the scaffold at Fotheringhay Castle.

Froude makes Mary's captivity and death the dramatic heart of his work. Letters, plots, and trials build toward the fatal warrant and its signing. Statecraft and tragedy merge in his telling of the affair. The volume shows his gifts at their height. Deep research in the archives weds a storyteller's sense of doom, pity, and high political stakes.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-6:

Edward Gibbon's sixth and final volume, with Milman's notes, opens at chapter fifty-nine with the Crusades. The Fourth Crusade follows, diverted to Constantinople, and chapter sixty-one narrates the partition of the Byzantine empire by French and Venetians. Greek emperors at Nicaea and the Latin emperors occupy the next chapters.

Gibbon then ranges over the Mongols, Timur's world-shaking campaigns, the Ottoman Turks, and the final siege of Constantinople in 1453, closing with Rome's ruins and his famous reflections among them. Timur meditating at Smyrna shows the sweep. Seventy-one chapters end here: the history that began with the Antonines concludes with an empire fallen and a city twice transformed.
humboldt-personal-narrative-williams-vol:
Volume six of Humboldt's Personal Narrative, in Helen Maria Williams's translation, appeared in 1826. The expedition moves from the Andes toward Peru and the Pacific coast. Humboldt's survey of Spanish America nears its close; Mexico and the voyage home lie just beyond this volume's edge.

He studies Lima, the cold ocean current that now bears his name, and the guano riches of the coast. Quito's volcanoes get their measurements, and the party descends toward the sea. As always, plants, rocks, stars, and politics share the page. The English set, running since 1814, had made Humboldt a household name among readers of science.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-6:
Satire and breakthrough share the sixth volume of Archer's 1908 Ibsen. The League of Youth mocks small-town political ambition, while Pillars of Society turns on a shipowner whose respectable front conceals corruption. Together they catch the moment Ibsen turned from historical verse toward the modern world.

In Pillars of Society, Consul Bernick's lies about his ships and his past slowly close around him. Exposure threatens everything until confession breaks the spell, a pattern later plays would darken. The League of Youth, lighter in touch, still stings any age that knows machine politics. Critics treat the volume as a hinge in theater history. After these plays, modern drama had found its road.
jataka-cowell-vol-6:
Volume six, from 1907, completes Cowell's English Jataka, the first full translation of the Buddha's birth stories. The closing tales are the longest and grandest of the 547. Chief among them is the Vessantara Jataka, the last birth before the Buddha's final life.

Prince Vessantara gives away everything: his wealth, his kingdom's rain-bringing elephant, and at last his own children and wife. His total generosity is the summit of the virtues the whole cycle teaches. The tale is still acted and painted across Southeast Asia each year. With it, Cowell's twelve-year labor closes the great story treasury of Buddhism.
lecky-england-18th-vol-6:
War with Napoleonic France fills the sixth volume of Lecky's History, from 1890. Trafalgar secures the seas, while the Peninsular campaign bleeds armies in Spain. Waterloo then ends the long struggle and frees a continent from a tyrant's grip at last.

Lecky tells England's supreme trial with fitting gravity throughout. Liberty strains under taxes, press gangs, and laws against dissent. Endurance, more than brilliance, forms his theme for these years. The volume traces the making of Britain's later greatness in fire. A free state survived total war without wholly losing its soul, in his sober view.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-6:

memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-montesp:

merivale-romans-empire-vol-6:
Reform and conversion mark the sixth volume of Merivale's History, from 1865. Diocletian rebuilds the state with stern new systems of rule and tax. Constantine then makes the Empire Christian, turning Western history onto a wholly new course within one lifetime.

Merivale brings his great work to the threshold of the medieval world. Ancient Rome ends here, and something new begins in its place. He tells the hinge of Western history with grace and care. The volume shows the rescue of a failing empire. It also shows a Christian order born, one that would outlast Rome itself.
nasa-tm-19710010488-msc-apollo-13-invest:
Panel 6 of the Manned Spacecraft Center Apollo 13 Investigation Team wrote this related systems evaluation. Volume 3 covers the Command and Service Module, the spacecraft whose oxygen tank failed in April 1970. The panel checked other parts and systems for the same kind of hidden failure risk.

The volume opens with the module pressure vessel, then gives a long subsystem by subsystem assessment. Later sections weigh how much damage each failure could cause. The report closes with conclusions and recommendations. It shows how investigators widened the Apollo 13 inquiry from one broken tank to the safety of the whole spacecraft.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-6:
Volume six of Schaff's Nicene Fathers, first series, turns from Augustine the fighter to Augustine the pastor. It holds his work on the Sermon on the Mount, his Harmony of the Gospels, and his homilies on the Gospels. The volume appeared in 1886.

On the Sermon on the Mount reads Christ's teaching as the charter of the Christian life, line by line. The Harmony then weaves the four evangelists into one account, answering readers troubled by their differences. The homilies show the bishop preaching to his people at Hippo in plain, urgent speech. The volume is the gentlest Augustine in the series.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-6:
Jerome, the great scholar monk of Bethlehem, fills volume six of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890, with his principal works. Jerome translated the Bible into Latin, the version the West used for a thousand years. Schaff and Wace edited the series.

The volume centers on his letters, the liveliest surviving from the ancient church: to widows, virgins, pupils, and rivals. He advises on study, fasting, grief, and the raising of girls, all in prose that sparkles and stings. His treatises against Helvidius and Jovinian defend the ascetic life he preached. No father is better company, or worse tempered. The volume is Jerome in full.
odd-man-out-sailor-s-knots-part-6:
William Wymark Jacobs wrote Odd Man Out as a comic tale. It is part six of Sailor's Knots, printed in 1909. A night watchman tells the story in his own voice. He warns that friendship can be a snare. He recalls shipmates Ted Denver and Charlie Brice.

The two friends shared money, lodging, and tobacco for years. People called them the Siamese twins for their closeness. Then a young woman entered their lives. Jacobs uses the tale to test loyalty and jealousy. The humor rests on plain speech and human folly. The watchman's blunt talk gives the tale much of its charm.

over-the-side-captains-all-book-6:
W. W. Jacobs tells Over the Side as a man who went to sea at fifteen. His father would not apprentice him to it, so he shipped before the mast. Seamen, he begins, are the class most prone to superstition. They float on black water with strange creatures below. One incident made him chary of calling any man a fool.

He shipped on the brig Endeavour, bound for Riga, under a fine skipper. A brawny, good-natured shipmate named Bill Smith protected him. The crew's one spiteful man was Jem Dadd. Dadd loved frightening his fellows with the supernatural. He would never let a rat be killed: rats were drowned sailors' souls, he claimed. Six or seven days out, something strange happened on Dadd's watch. The tale is Jacobs in his night-watch vein.
pausanias-description-greece-frazer-vol-:

A full index turns thousands of pages into a searchable reference. Closing commentary gathers Frazer's final judgments on the traveler and his world. Six volumes amount to the most complete guide ever made to ancient Greece. Frazer's labor stretched across years of translation and verification. Modern digital searches have replaced the index's function, not its scholarship. The set still sits on the shelves of every serious classical library.
personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-volume-:
Part 6 of volume 2 of Sheridan's memoirs opens at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, in September 1867. Sheridan takes command of a department covering Missouri, Kansas, the Indian Territory, and New Mexico. West of the Missouri, he writes, Native peoples had grown restless as the Pacific railroads crossed their hunting-grounds and pioneers poured into Kansas and Colorado.

The chapter promises the Treaty of Medicine Lodge, raids, the death of the scout Comstock, and preparations for a winter campaign. Buffalo Bill appears, undertaking a dangerous task. These pages show the cavalry general turned frontier commander, in the hardest of his peacetime assignments.
personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-6:
Part 6 of Grant's memoirs opens at chapter sixty-two, with Sherman in possession of Savannah. Grant confesses he never originally meant Sherman to march north through the Carolinas. He had collected transports to carry the army by sea to the James River, until Sherman proposed the march and Grant gladly approved it.

The reasoning is strategic and unsparing: Georgia's railroads already destroyed, the Carolinas must be made helpless to feed Lee's army, shrinking Richmond's supply ground to exhausted Virginia. This final part, with footnotes for the whole work, carries the war to its end under Grant's direction.
ranke-history-england-vol-6:
Civil war, Cromwell, and Restoration close Ranke's History in Volume 6. The 1875 Oxenford translation ends the six-book span of England's turmoil. Charles II returns to the throne as the great tale resolves.

Ranke passes cool judgment on the whole English revolution here. He weighs king, army, and parliament in the scales of Europe. Cromwell's rule gets firm, fair treatment from the German master's pen. The republic fails, the monarchy returns, and old wounds stay open. Few historians of the age command such range or such calm. The final volume takes the measure of England's most wild century.
samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-6:

Miss Timson's letter was written to Samantha on the sixth day of his sickness, and Josiah and Samantha set sail for Loontown on the day after they got it. Samantha laid the case before the female sisters of the meeting house, and they all counselled her to go. Sister Bobbet had fallen on the apple parings, so the work of papering the meeting house could not go on in any case. The interests of Zion, the sisters said, would not languish on account of her absence for a day or two.

The errand to Loontown, all the sisters agreed, was a fair and square case of duty, though they divided on almost everything else.

the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-6:
Part six of Mark Twain's The Adventures of Tom Sawyer opens at chapter twenty-three, when the sleepy village air is stirred hard by the murder trial. The trial at once becomes the one topic of talk in St. Petersburg.

Each mention of the murder sends a shudder to Tom's heart, since his conscience reads each remark as a feeler aimed at him. He cannot see how he could be guessed to know of the crime, yet he stays in a cold shiver. He draws Huck to a lonely place to unseal his tongue and split his load of dread. Readers watch Tom weigh his oath of silence against an innocent man, Muff Potter, in the dock.

All wait to welcome Admiral Prince Philip d'Avranche, Duc de Bercy, and to offer a bounty to Jerseymen who enlist under him. Chapbooks tell of French defeats and the sea fight that made Philip an admiral. Yet Philip and his flag lieutenant do not arrive. The Comtesse Chantavoine sits outwardly calm while officials whisper and crowds grow restless.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-3-no-6:

Quackery, he says, may win wealth in other callings, but shallowness cannot pass for depth before a sharp bench and watchful rivals. Every cause sets one attorney as a sentinel upon the other, so slips are exposed at once. A lawyer's public standing, in this view, is a sifted judgment formed after severe trial, fitting praise for Paine's career.
the-bequest-ship-s-company-part-6:
W. W. Jacobs placed a tale called The Bequest in his Ship's Company collection. Robert Clarkson sits by his fire after the funeral of his lifelong neighbour and successful rival in love. The dead man, Phipps, had won the woman both men courted thirty years earlier.

A doleful visitor, Mr Smithson, calls to ask how Clarkson bears up and hints that he will have her at last. Clarkson answers that this was the dead man's wish. Yet anger grows when he reveals the provision left behind: only furniture and fifty pounds of insurance money. A bequest meant as generosity begins to look like a burden.
the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-volum: Volume 6 of Charles James Lever's Confessions of Harry Lorrequer, printed at Dublin in 1839, is shown here by front matter alone in this record. the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-6:
Volume six of The Doré Gallery of Bible Illustrations opens with the Nativity. The text follows Luke: Caesar's decree sends Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, where her son is born and laid in a manger for lack of room at the inn. Shepherds in the fields hear an angel bring good tidings of great joy, then a host of heaven sings.

The shepherds hurry to see the child. Doré's engraving bathes the stable in soft light. With this volume the gallery turns from Israel's kings and prophets to the life of Christ.
the-gilded-age-part-6:
Part 6 of The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today is dated 1873. Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner wrote the novel. This part opens with Chapter XLVI. Philip Sterling walks up Pennsylvania Avenue with Senator Dilworthy. It is a bright spring morning. Peach trees are in bloom. The air is soft after a long night in the chamber.

Dilworthy calls the night's work a gift from Providence. A new school plan has passed one house. He says Laura Hawkins will be almost rich if the Hawkins claim holds. Philip asks a plain question. Will the family see much of the cash? The senator looks hard at him. Then he swears he has kept their good at heart all along.
the-great-conspiracy-volume-6:
John Logan wrote The Great Conspiracy: Its Origin and History. This record is Part 6 of that work. It opens with Chapter XXII, Freedom's Sun Still Rising. After Lincoln issued the Proclamation of Emancipation, the friends of freedom saw a danger. Until that act was written into the Constitution itself, there could be no real assurance of safety for the freed. A living spark of dissension would be left. It might at any time be fanned again into civil war.

Lincoln, Logan says, favored and even urged action by Congress at all proper times. Congress was slow. Definite action came only in the following year. Lincoln found it needful to speak in his third Annual Message. While he remained in his position, he said, he would not retract or modify the Emancipation Proclamation. The chapter carries the fight from the proclamation toward a constitutional amendment.
the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1620-m: A Project Gutenberg header is all that stands in this record for volume 6 of The Mayflower and Her Log by Azel Ames. the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-volume-6: The pages present for volume 6 of George Meredith's The Ordeal of Richard Feverel hold nothing but the Project Gutenberg header. the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-6:
Part 6 of Mark Twain's The Prince and the Pauper opens at Chapter XVIII, The Prince with the Tramps. The troop of vagabonds turns out at dawn under a lowering sky, sloppy ground underfoot and a winter chill in the air. Gaiety is gone. The Ruffler puts Jack, the disguised king, in Hugo's charge and warns him not to be too rough. John Canty is ordered to keep away from the boy.

As the weather mildens, the gang's spirits rise into insolence. Passengers give them the road and take their ribaldry meekly. They snatch linen from hedges in full view of owners too afraid to protest. At a farmhouse they make themselves at home while the trembling family empties the larder for their breakfast. They throw bones at the farmer and butter the head of a daughter who resents them. They threaten to burn the house if word reaches the authorities.
the-three-sisters-night-watches-part-6:
W. W. Jacobs begins The Three Sisters, from his Night Watches, at a deathbed thirty years before a wet autumn evening. Ursula Mallow, eldest of three sisters at Mallett's Lodge, lies behind dingy moth-eaten curtains under a smoking oil-lamp. She commands her sister Tabitha that nothing is to be changed. Her room must stay locked and unopened forever. Tabitha answers brusquely that it cannot matter to her then.

Ursula insists it does matter, for she is certain she will sometimes visit the house again and watch over them both. She kisses weeping Eunice and promises to come for each sister in turn when her lease of life runs out. Then the lamp goes suddenly out. Jacobs blends his usual dry comedy of character with a genuine ghost-story chill, letting a domineering sister rule from beyond the grave.
the-works-of-lord-byron-vol-6: Poetry volume six of Byron's works, edited by Ernest Hartley Coleridge in 1903, is shown through front pages only. The edition is dedicated to Algernon Charles Swinburne. Transcriber notes explain how Greek passages were handled. They appear as Beta-code transliterations in the electronic text. Long and short vowels are marked with brackets. Notes also praise the edition's copious footnotes. The poem itself does not begin within the pages present here.
thirlwall-history-greece-vol-6:
Volume 6 of Thirlwall's History, from 1845, walks through the war's wreckage. Lysander triumphs, and the Thirty Tyrants seize Athens in his wake. The death of Socrates closes the book's span of bitter years.

Thirlwall keeps his usual fairness amid ruin, revenge, and fear. Democracy falls, returns, then judges its greatest critic to death. He lets readers weigh each act without pushing them to a side. The Greeks must live with what they have done to themselves. His steady hand guides readers through tangled trials and coups alike. The morning after disaster has seldom been told so clearly.
un-ga-res-31-6:
South Africa's plan to carve black homelands out of its map drew a flat refusal in Resolution 31/6, adopted by the General Assembly in 1976. The apartheid state had declared the Transkei, the first of its so-called bantustans, free on 26 October 1976. A vote of the year before had already condemned the whole scheme. Reports of the Assembly's anti-apartheid team lay before it.

The bantustans are condemned in the strongest terms. They were built, the text holds, to lock apartheid in place, to break the land's unity, and to strip the African people of their rights while white rule lasts. The Transkei's claimed freedom is rejected as void. All states are called to grant it no respect of any kind.
un-ga-res-6: War relief still hung over Europe when the General Assembly passed Resolution 6 on 1 February 1946. The relief agency UNRRA was set to end its work in Europe by the close of 1946, and in the Far East by March 1947. A new team was formed for two tasks. It would press states that had signed the UNRRA deal but not yet paid the fresh sums asked of them in 1945. It would also urge UN members outside the deal to join it.
un-ga-res-a-69-6: Sport can build peace, holds Resolution A/69/6, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the chain of votes since 2003 that treat sport as a tool for schools, health, growth, and peace. The year 2005 was kept as the world year of sport. Each 6 April now serves as the world day of sport for growth and peace, and the Secretary-General's report on the gains of sport is noted with thanks.
un-ga-res-es-11-6:
One year into Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the General Assembly set out its terms for peace in Resolution ES-11/6, adopted on 23 February 2023. Its head names the point: the Charter's own rules are the base for a full, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine. The ban on force against the land or freedom of any state is recalled. So is the rule that no land gain won by force may be held as lawful.

The text recalls the past votes of the emergency session, and the 2014 vote on Crimea. A just peace, it holds, would be a great gain for peace in the whole world. The world court's order of March 2022, which told Russia to halt its attack, is recalled as well. The terms are drawn from the Charter, not from the gun.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 31/6, adopted in parts on 26 October and 9 November 1976, is a wide set of texts on South Africa under the heading Situation of South Africa. Its first part strongly condemned the bantustans. It rejected the claimed independence of the Transkei and declared it invalid. It told all governments to give it no recognition and no dealings.

Later parts backed the United Nations Trust Fund for South Africa. They voiced support for South African political prisoners after the Soweto killings, and demanded their release. Others pressed the Security Council for a binding arms ban. Others condemned joint work between Israel and South Africa. Others backed a boycott of apartheid in sports.

The General Assembly adopted resolution 6 (I) on 29 January 1946 to chase down unpaid pledges to the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration. It creates a five-member committee, appointed by the Assembly's President in consultation with the Secretary-General, to press member states for outstanding contributions and report back to the Assembly's next session. The committee works as UNRRA's relief operations wind down in Europe at the end of 1946 and in the Far East in early 1947.

General Assembly resolution 69/6 (2014) promotes sport as a means to advance education, health, development, and peace. The Assembly invites member states, United Nations bodies, sports organizations, and the private sector to work with the United Nations Office on Sport for Development and Peace. It invites them to mainstream sport in development policies and use major events to build inclusion. It welcomes the April 2014 memorandum between the United Nations and the International Olympic Committee, and looks ahead to the Rio 2016 Games. It supports the autonomy of sport and the Olympic movement.

UN General Assembly Resolution ES-11/6 — the 2023 emergency-session resolution on the principles for peace in Ukraine. It restated the Charter’s demands a year into the war. The 2023 peace principles is the restated Charter: the UN Charter’s demands formally renewed.
un-sc-res-6: New members would be judged on a fixed clock under Security Council Resolution 6 of 1946. Membership in the UN stands open, under Article 4 of the Charter, to all peace-loving states that take up its duties. The General Assembly would meet again on 3 September 1946 to act on bids. The Council rules that bids will be weighed at meetings in August of that year, held for that task alone. Bids sent in before 15 July go first to a team drawn from all Council members.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
In 1946, the first year of the United Nations, states were already applying to join the new organization. The General Assembly would meet that autumn to admit new members, acting on the Council's recommendation. Resolution 6 sets the timetable for handling those applications.

Applications received by the Secretary-General would be examined by the Council at meetings in August 1946, held for that purpose. Applications received before 15 July 1946 would go first to a committee. The committee had one representative from each member of the Council. It had to report back by 1 August 1946. That timing would let the General Assembly act on the bids when it met. The text is an early piece of procedure, from the months when the United Nations was still building its own routines.
vittoria-volume-6: The sixth volume of George Meredith's Vittoria, number 46 in the Gutenberg Meredith series, presents only the project's old header in these pages.
